I think the Solicitor General has made the case still worse. The minister went to Spain and enjoyed a very nice vacation in that country. We cannot afford these things with the budget of Canada in its present position. We cannot afford to create a new commission when we already have a competent body in the Department of Marine. This department is made up of Canadians and it seems to me to be a mistake to employ a stranger to come to tell us what to do. The government is trying to get away from governmental and parliamentary responsibility. This commission is to receive the money of Canadians and is to spend it as it likes subject to the approval of the governor in council. Parliament will have nothing to say. We are running away from our responsibility. When we go back to our constituencies and hear complaints of the radio commission we must tell our people that even though we have their mandate to represent them in this house, we 'have nothing to do with the matter, it rests in the hands of three appointees. That will not work at all. Canadians are accustomed to responsible government but I am sorry to say 'that we are drifting away from it. There will finally be a revulsion in public opinion throughout the whole of Canada and a desire to go back to parliamentary representation and parliamentary government. We have received the mandate of the people to act for them and we will have to account for all these commissions. Thirty-three years ago when I was a young member of parliament the people could say to me: you are young and active and you can do things; we trust you. But to-dav they say: you are powerless, everything is in 
the hands of a radio commission, a soldiers' commission, a pension commission and a civil service commission. We are departing from that most sacred of principles, parliamentary control and parliamentary responsibility.
The Solicitor General is a man of learning and a man of letters and he remembers the fight which took place in Ontario, Quebec and the maritime provinces to obtain parliamentary government and parliamentary responsibility. We are drifting back to the old days when the government with a selfappointed council could dispose of the moneys of the people and the representatives of the people had nothing to say. We can remember when the representatives in the legislature at Quebec were debarred from voting a dollar of public money. Is it the ambition of hon. friends opposite to return to such a form of government? I hope not. They are Canadians like ourselves, they are proud of the position which Canada occupies as the foremost sister nation of the empire and we should not override, overrule and overthrow the sacred principles of responsible government in order to make a few political appointments which will mostly be wiped out by the incoming administration. Hon. friends opposite are reasonable men. Do they think that Canada will stand for long for the position in which this government is at the present time? The salaries of the members of the tariff board are being increased while the members of the old tariff board were dismissed twenty-four hours after this party came into power. This new board is to be merely a fact finding body, it will have no responsibility or power except to report to the government. The government can do what it likes with its recommendations. The salaries of these men are being increased when the men and women of Canada, the charwomen, the members of parliament and the civil servants have had their salaries decreased. All statutory increases have been withheld for the last two years.
I am sorry that the Prime Minister of Canada, talented as he is, patriotic as I think he is, has come forward and set such an example to the people of Canada. Ho has stated that there are two measures which shall apply; if a man occupies an exalted position, he is entitled to an increase in salary but if he does not occupy such a position, he will have to take a cut. This session we are voting 870,000,000 in new taxes. I wish hon. members would come down to the part of the country I represent to see the conditions which prevail. There has not been a sawmill in operation for the last two years; taxes have not

We have even reached the bench, the most sacred institution we have in this country. Outstanding men are to be forced to retire from their judicial offices in order that new judges may be appointed by this government. The Prime Minister is a distinguished lawyer and I can remember his saying when in opposition that no appointee of his would be raised to the bench except for his judicial qualifications. It is unfortunate for the Prime Minister that he should be presiding over the destinies of Canada at the most unfavourable time in its whole history, and apparently he is trying to undo much of what he did in 1930. During the short session of 1930 he came here and raised the tariff probably thinking it would bring about what he had in view. But what has been the result? Since that time he has been trying to undo what was done in 1930, first with the mother country, to-morrow probably with the United States and the day after perhaps with France. He is trying to get back to the policy of the liberal party which is the policy of all the men who have led Canada. Canada cannot be self-contained. Canada cannot live by itself. What do we need at the present time? Markets, and nothing but markets.

It is unfortunate that the radio commission has been made a purely political combination, that its personnel should be political appointees, and that now the radio commission should be trying to evade the Civil Service Act by making all its appointments independent of the Civil Service Commission. It is unfortunate because such a policy will be condemned by at least half the population of Canada, and by its present policy this government is condemning the traditional policy of the Conservative party as it was laid down in 1918 by Sir Robert Borden, then leader of that party, when he brought the outside service under the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Cimmission.

Mr. Speaker, my criticism of this bill is in the main confined to the first section. Had it not been for that I think I could have seen my way clear to have supported the other two clauses. Like the majority of the members of this

'house I gave hearty support to ithe principle of national control of our broadcasting system. There is no occasion at this time to go into the reasons why we thought that .that was the best system for the Canadian people. I still believe, in spite of some of the difficulties that have arisen, that our hopes lie in that direction. It is true that difficulties have arisen. Perhaps that is inevitable in view of the fact that we have to trust .the oarrying out of our ideals to weak and imperfect human instruments, and it may always be that way.
Criticism has been made of conditions prevailing in broadcasting in the west, and particularly in Saskatchewan. For my part I am prepared to recognize that fact so far as the technical end of the work is concerned. My thought is that if we fail to give the commission the finances for which they are asking at the present time, possibly we may only prolong this period of inconvenience and dissatisfaction. So on that point I am not going to offer any criticism.
I think we have some reason, however, to suppose that from another standpoint the commission is deserving of criticism. Certain public statements which the chairman of the commission has made would indicate that in some respects he is not temperamentally fitted to be at the head of the commission, for he seems inclined to resent, and to rush into print to repudiate, any statements that are made in criticism of his actions. Being a public servant he will have to learn to take criticism without being too ready to rush into print. The very fact that he was reported the other day to have said that anybody who criticized the radio commission on the ground that it was not functioning properly was either a liar or a fool indicates that the chairman needs a little advice as to that courtesy which is due to the public from a man occupying the position he does. However, as I said, I have an objection to raise to the first section of the bill, and it is to the proposal that the employees of the commission shall be chosen purely at the will of

the radio commission, that appointments shall be taken out entirely from under the control of the Civil Service Commission. This radio commission is to be given the power to set up an entirely new organization of its own in spite of the fact that we already have in the employ of the government men who are well qualified from their experience to deal with these matters. What does that mean? It means the possibility of the setting up of a very expensive organization, and if that organization is set up without any control by parliament we have reason to suppose that at least it might become so expensive that the people of Canada would not be able to bear the expenditure, and we might be faced later on with the proposal to raise the licence fee, which has already been raised from one to two dollars. Who knows, if we put into the hands of the radio commission the power to create such an organization as I have suggested, that it might not become so expensive that the people of Canada would rise in revolt against the whole system and would recede from the position we have taken, which I think is endorsed by the great majority of the people of this country, that radio should be under the control of a national system. So there lies in this the danger of completely destroying our national system of broadcasting. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, and for that only, I feel I cannot give my support to this bill. For the reasons I have indicated other sections of the bill may commend themselves to me, especially in view of the fact that as soon as possible the disabilities arising from unsatisfactory methods of broadcasting must be removed.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister if he has taken cognizance of section 3 subparagraph 14 of the bill. I believe in this paragraph he is creating a precedent that is bound to have an ill effect on every department of government. He wall recall that during the present session of parliament the Minister of Justice introduced a bill to modify the mounted police legislation and to authorize the department to spend, over and above the estimates voted by parliament, whatever revenues would accrue. I objected to that part of the bill, and it was withdrawn.
To-day we are doing exactly the same thing. We are authorizing the radio commission to expend money voted by parliament, and they are being given the right by statute to expend sums of money over and above estimates voted by parliament, and without the control of parliament. I believe the Prime Minister will readily realize that such a precedent

Radio Broadcasting Act
would be detrimental to other departments. No other department has been granted the right to expend moneys which have accrued through revenues. As a rule all these receipts are credited to the receiver general.
Such a provision obtained last year with regard1 to the radio commission. The Prime Minister himself told us that the appropriations voted for the radio commission represented the income received from the sale of licences, and that in no way shape or form would the moneys received from radio licences be exceeded. Here however we are authorizing the commission to spend money voted by parliament, and beyond that we are creating two sets of estimates for the department, one voted by parliament yearly, and the other consisting of money which will accrue from rendering services mentioned in the bill. It is quite true that in the next section further provisions are made concerning appropriations. We must remember however that these moneys divide themselves into two classes, one being the estimates voted yearly by parliament representing the income received from the sale of radio licences, and the remainder money the commission will have the right to spend without the authority of parliament. I am calling the attention of the Prime Minister to this fact because in the house we have always fought shy of authorizing any department of the crown to spend money, from whatever source, except that voted by parliament.

Mr. Speaker, as a member of the committee on radio which sat last year I should like to offer one or two observations on the bill. Those of us who were members of the committee and did not belong to the party in power were, I believe, entirely fair in our attitude when we supported the idea of the nationalization of radio as a great public benefit and public utility. There was no difference of opinion, and we supported the report unanimously. Again in the house we supported the bill unanimously, when it was introduced by the Prime Minister. I 'aim still one hundred per cent in favour of the nationalization of radio. I say without any intention of giving offence that I am not quite satisfied with matters as the5'' have been conducted by the commission. I am willing to make due allowance, and to admit that possibly the commission has not had sufficient time to make good on the work which they have undertaken. As I say, I am quite willing to make some allowance in that regard. I should like to say, further, without intending to give offence to the Prime Minister that I believe he made an error in making appointments, and that the public, and perhaps parties opposed to him, lost just a bit of confidence in the genuineness of the statements made by the government to the effect that politics would not enter into the work of the radio broadcasting commission.
As I said before, we accepted in good faith all assurances, and embodied in the report a clause to the effect that there should be no political influence of any kind either in appointments to the board or in the conduct of the work of the commission, after it had been established. I criticized, as did some other members, the appointment of one of the members of the commission-not on any score of policy, but because it did not seem to me to be in accord with the report of the committee, or with the promises made by the Prime Minister, when the bill was in the house, to the effect that there would foe no political influence in connection with appointments.
I cannot agree with the Prime Minister in his definition of what constitutes a political appointment. I will say that I have had a short meeting with one of the commissioners, to whom reference has often been made, the gentleman from the province of Quebec, and I had the pleasure of receiving his assurance in the presence of other hon. members in the committee to the effect that so far as he was concerned no political influence would be wielded in carrying on the work of the commission. In the meantime, at least, I am willing to take him at his word. I think at the outset one mistake was made.
What does the hon. member propose to do with politicians who are out of a job?

I would elect them to parliament. The chief point of contention in regard to this bill seems to be that there has been a political bias exercised in appointments and in the work of the commission. Very naturally, denials have been made by the government. I do not .believe-and I do not blame the commission for this, but mention it at this time so 'that it may serve as a warning in the future-that the granting of the licence to or what took place subsequently in connection with the Windsor radio station was entirely free of party politics. I make that statement, trusting that in future, whatever the commission may do, it will see to it that there will be no further interference, so far as political influence is concerned. I am willing to say that as only three or four months have elapsed since the commission was appointed, it is not reasonable to expect that within such a short time they can properly
Radio Broadcasting Act

rearrange the whole system of radio distribution so that everybody will be satisfied, or so that we will have a perfect system of radio broadcasting. That is not to be expected and for my part I am inclined to be liberal and to make allowance for the difficulties of the work which has to be done.
I find that the bill deals with three things. First it proposes to take from the purview of the Civil Service Commission the appointment of all employees connected with the work of the radio commission. Secondly, it proposes to vest in the governor in council the approval of all capital expenditures in connection with broadcasting stations. And lastly, although I am not quite clear as to the meaning of the third clause, it proposes to give to the commission the right to expend all moneys they receive-I presume by way of licence fees, or revenues received from advertising, and so on. I have not a great deal of fault to find with the last dause, because when the committee drew up its report I favoured the principle that the commission should collect the licence fees. I feel that if it were a responsible commission, a good commission, a commission that wanted to do its duty, it should be entrusted with the work of collecting the licence fees and expending the money for the purpose for which the commission was created. I do not entirely agree with some of my hon. friends on this side that all those moneys must necessarily be voted by parliament. The commission would be limited absolutely to the amount of licence fees which it collects and can spend no more. I can see no very good reason why we should depart from the principle that is observed in the conduct of the Canadian National Railways. Ever since we took over the national railways the revenues collected by those railways in the ordinary conduct of business, charges for freight, passengers and so on, were expended by the board of the railway without reference to the House of Commons. I have not a great deal of fault to find with that, because I believe that if you have a commission worth its salt, one that should have encouragement to go on and do a good job, you have to give it a certain freedom of action. If i't is not deserving of such freedom then, of course, it should be replaced.
With regard to the sections of the bill-I am taking them in reverse order-I know they are the result of the recommendations of Major Cdadstone Murray, an expert adviser who comes from the British Broadcasting Corporation and has made an investigation into the Canadian situation. I receive these recommendations with a great deal of respect, but

I am constrained to say that merely because Major Murray made them it does not necessarily follow that we must approve of them in every particular. In conversation with him the other day and with some of my colleagues on that committee this matter came up; I cannot see why all the employees of the radio broadcasting commission should be removed from the control of the Civil Service Commission. I quite grant this, that as far as the technical advisers and technical officers and artists are concerned there is good reason why the commission itself should make those appointments. I should say the commission should make them. But when you come to the clerical staff, stenographers and so on-
Secretaries.

Secretaries if you like, and clerks engaged in the office of the commission, I see no reason why they should not be subject to appointment by the Civil Service Commission just the same as similar employees in any other department of the government. While it may not mean a very great deal at this time, while the number of employees is not very great, this matter of radio broadcasting is a very big thing and may expand in such a way that in time there will be a great many employees. I think there is real cause for criticism by those on this side who believe that, whether or not it will be exercised, there is at least room under this provision for the exercise of political patronage. For my part, as I have said from the beginning, I would like to see as many opportunities as possible for the exercise of such patronage removed. The radio broadcasting commission cannot be as successful as it ought to be if any government exercises political patronage in the conduct of such a national undertaking.
As far as the substitution of the governor in council for the parliament of Canada is concerned in the matter of expenditures on capital account, I have not a very great deal to say except again I do not see why we should depart from the principle that we observe in connection with the Canadian National Railways. When the Canadian National Railways require appropriations for capital expenditures they go not to the governor in council, but to the parliament of Canada, and properly so. I see no reason for varying that practice. The only apparent reason that was given I think was that since parliament meets only once a year and there is an interval of perhaps seven or eight months when parliament is no't in session, and

Radio Broadcasting Act
the commission might find it necessary to acquire a station here or there or perhaps build a station, it would be prejudicial to the work of the commission if they had to wait until parliament met to get an appropriation for capital expenditure. There may be a little weight in that argument, but I do not think there is enough to justify us in violating the principle.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, while in some respects I am in favour of the provisions of the bill, I feel that the government might very well make a distinction as far as appointments are concerned, they could segregate the technical officers and have those appointed by the radio commission itself but as far as other clerical employees are concerned they could leave them for appointment by the Civil Service Commission. And they should make no change as far as capital expenditures are concerned but should have those authorized by parliament in the same manner as capital expenditures are authorized for the Canadian National Railways.
Hon. RAYMOND D. MORAND (East Essex): Mr. Speaker, I wish to take a very few minutes to discuss one or two phases of this situation. The main criticisms that are offered at the present time to this bill are only two or three; one the appointment to the commission of a man with some political background. Now I have been in the house long enough and I know my own people long enough to realize that as it was necessary to appoint one French-Canadian upon that commission I doubt very much if you could find one who had not been in politics somewhere. I am quite sure that hon. members on the other side would not expect us to take one of their friends particularly, consequently, we have taken one from this side. However, that is not a new principle, that applies to the appointment of our judges, and I am sure we cannot and will not say that our judges are guided by political consideration in their judgments or the work that they do.
Another thing I find a little difficult to get quite straight in my mind is the objection that the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) has to the station at Windsor. He complains that there was some political bias in respect to this station. There were two stations in that part of the country, that were thought to be somewhat political, but they were amalgamated and now there is only one. Is there no way to please hon. gentlemen opposite? Even for removing them they still find fault.
A fact that appears to be overlooked in respect to this question is that radio broadcasting is a business. It is not a department of government, it is purely a business. The hon. member for North Waterloo in connection with two of the clauses of this bill made reference to the Canadian National Railways. Why not carry the principle a little further? To my mind it is just as sensible to say that the Civil Service Commission should appoint the men working for the Canadian National as those employed by this commission. Can one conceive of the Civil Service Commission holding an examination for a prima donna for instance or someone who is going to appear before the microphone at a broadcasting station? The thing on the face of it is ridiculous. It might be that for a few appointments here in Ottawa such as stenographers, and so on, the Civil Service Commission might act, but from time to time this business of broadcasting will be taking over stations throughout Canada, will be employing technical men and artists, consequently it is surely ridiculous to think that the Civil Service Commission must pass upon whether these people can or cannot be hired and appear, or shall have their salaries set by the Civil Service Commission.
I made an exception in the case of the technical officers.

Well, others did not. To me that is so evident that I cannot imagine why such an argument is made. The Civil Sendee Commission are not losing anything they ever had, because they have never had anything to do with this new business. Again I say one might just as well expect them to appoint the engineers, firemen, switchmen and so on all over the Canadian National system.

feature is concerned, it is simply a question of making definite the ideas which were both understood and written in the report which was unanimously brought into this house. The intention was, and I believe still is-and I think the feeling is quite unanimous-that money received from the broadcasting business should be used in order to give Canada proper programs and proper radio stations. That is all that is done here.
With regard to paragraph 2, I do not think it makes a great deal of difference in the practical working out of the matter whether parliament or the governor in council has this power; what goes to the governor in
Radio Broadcasting Act

council usually comes to parliament later, so practically there is not a great deal of difference.
We have been hearing a great deal with regard to changes in wave lengths and interference. Certainly there will be trouble. I do not think anything could better justify the action taken by the committee last year than this tremendous effort that is being made to halt the nationalization of broadcasting. It is my firm belief that if this action had not been taken last year it never would have been taken in Canada, because the opposition has been very great. It took a government with a great deal of courage to put through the nationalization scheme last year. Personally I am just as strong now in my belief that this is the proper way to handle the radio situation, and I think in all fairness we can ask the members of this house and the people of Canada to give the commission a chance to work out its own salvation and deal with a most difficult problem, even though there may be a good deal of trouble during the period of transition.

I wish the minister would say something in that regard.
In vieiw of the fact that the minister did not say anything in that regard I will tell the hon. member that this is one of the most important sections of the whole Dominion of Canada, and I think it is entitled to a first class radio station. Station CKOK is one of the best equipped radio stations in Canada, and if the hon. member had his ear to the ground he would cease his criticism of it. The hon. gentleman seeks to imply that station CKOK has been really a United States station, while the fact is that thirty-five of the forty-two employees of that station

Radio Broadcasting Act
are Canadian citizens and residents of this country. I have here many newspaper clippings, but I am going to read only one to prove that the hon. member, to use a slang expression, is all wet with regard to station CKOK. I quote again:
Politics and "Influence"
CKOK, the border's broadcasting station, is under fire from the stronghold of local opponents. The management of the station has been panned and accused because it broadcasts the programs of the Columbia network, a United States organization.
Operators of the station have been accused of using "political influence" to get the licence to operate. Rather amused are some of the onlookers, who recall the election of 1930. The Conservatives were far from satisfied at the treatment of a local organization which it is believed was promised the radio licence by Mr. King, the leader of the defeated party.
In the face of this, however, the present owners of the station are still accused of operating only through "political" influence.
I rise merely to put this clipping on record and to ask the hon. member for North Waterloo if he will not give us a little cooperation and support, instead of continuing to criticize one of the best radio stations in Canada, so that CKOK may have a fair trial and the people of western Ontario may have a station by means of which they can hear Canadian programs instead of being compelled to listen to United States programs all the time. Station CKOK has reached out and obtained business in the city of Detroit, and I believe the jealousy which has arisen because of that fact has been responsible for much of the opposition to this station.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who has just taken his seat has quoted something in which reference was made to myself as having promised to some one a radio licence or something of the kind. Seeing that I am in the house, and that it might in consequence be assumed that having listened to that quotation I agreed with it, I want to say now that never at any time, directly or indirectly, did I promise anyone anything of the sort or in that connection.

I gladly accept the statement of the right hon. gentleman, but let me say that rumors to this effect were circulated throughout the county of Essex prior to the election of 1930.
Mr. CAMERON R. McINTOSH (North Battleford):	Mr. Speaker, I rise to oppose
Bill No. 99, an act to aimend the Canadian Broadcasting Act, 1932. May I say that when the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific railway bill was before the house I opposed that measure. I opposed that legislation for more
than one reason. In the first place I took exception to iit because it came to the House of Commons in an indirect way. It came into this house through the Senate and my contention was that a bill of that nature ought to be brought before the Commons directly and not indirectly. I argued that it should first have come before the representatives of the people, men elected by the people, and not before the Senate, which is the result of indirect election. Because of the mistake by the government in that respect I opposed that irresponsible legislation. I opposed it for another reason, namely, that it was based on a report which had been prepared by a nonCanadian commission. The report was submitted by ,the Duff commission, which was not a full-fledged Canadian commission inasmuch as it included representatives from Great Britain and the United States. I pointed out that such representation was unnecessary, because in my opinion the time had come in the history of Canada when there was sufficient ability to be found right in this dominion to deal with matters affecting transportation and kindred subjects. I said that we should appoint our own board or commission, a purely Canadian body, to investigate the transportation problem and report accordingly.
I oppose the legislation now before us on somewhat the same grounds. I understand that there has been dragged into this discussion-and quite rightly-the report of Mr. Gladstone Murray, an expert of the British Broadcasting Corporation, a native Canadian but a man who thinks that there are some phases of the radio problem that ought not to be discussed in parliament. What an impossible thought! What will we hear next in this chamber. I differ entirely from that point of view; it is not the Canadian point of view. Every question touching the welfare of the Canadian people ought to be discussed in this house and settled by the representatives of the Canadian electorate, and we are in no need of experts, whether born within or outside of this country, to come to Canada and tell us what we should do-to tell us that the time has arrived when certain aspects of important parliamentary legislation ought not to be reviewed fully by the members in this chamber elected to represent the dominion as a whole.
I oppose this legislation for the further reason that there is an endeavour to take out of the hands of the Civil Service Commission appointments to the radio broadcasting commission. I do not believe that there is any support in the way of public opinion in Canada for action of that kind. I do not believe
Radio Broadcasting Act

there is support for it in the far west; certainly there is none in the middle west. Nor is there any support for it, in my opinion, in Ontario, Quebec or the maritime provinces. Consequently action of that kind is purely govermental, purely executive and partisan, and has no justification in public opinion.
Because these appointments are not to be left to the Civil Service Commission, because we are by this means doing our 'best to destroy the Civil Service Commission as a national organization that should function properly, because this bill proposes something that will militate against the successful operation of the Civil Service Commission, undermining its efficiency and permanency-because apparently my hon. friends are out to destroy it as far as possible by taking away from it the powers which it ought to exercise-I am opposed to the legislation which is now before the house. More than that, it seems to me that in the new section 14, subsection 1, wherein the expenditure of moneys is to be taken out of the hands of parliament, we are giving up one of the historic functions of parliamentary government. I cannot sanction anything that looks like a move in that direction. History tells us that parliament must have control of every dollar, every cent of revenue which is raised by taxes, and the moment we depart from that principle in the Slightest degree we are in danger of destroying parliamentary government in this country, and I am opposed to any move along that line. Further than that, if we are to have parliamentary government in Canada, parliamentary government worthy of the name, we must see to it that parliament exercises proper control over such matters. There should be no control through commissions, executives and experts. The best ex-,pert opinion in Canada can be found in this house; we do not need to import experts.

Is the hon. gentleman referring to himself?
No, I am referring to you.
You are doing well if that is what you mean.
I was judging by your own estimate of yourself.

I suggest that the hon. gentleman should try to estimate himself properly. He will have quite a job on his hands. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that if we have not full control in this house over the revenues of the country then we have not complete parliamentary government in Can-

ada, and any action on the part of any government that will tend to weaken parliament in this respect will meet with my opposition.
With regard to this bill, from the point of view of its effect on the Civil Service Commission, I have some information which I wish to put on Hansard. It brings out the political relationship that exists at the present time between the Civil Service Commission, the Px-ime Minister of Canada, the government of this country and those who are seeking positions on the radio commission. The information I want to put on the record is this:

I will not read the whole return, but there are a few parts of it that bear on the main problem before the house, namely, the attempt to make this radio commission a purely political body. If that effort continues then we might as well as a parliament scrap the Civil Service Commission at once and be through with it. I have here a return dated Ottawa, November 24, 1932, in which reference is made by Hector Charlesworbh, chairman of the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Commission, to organization work-organizing the commission, or in other words, dealing with the filling of key positions. The Prime Minister's name is mentioned in this return, and I shall read the document as it has been submitted to the house:
Ottawa, November 24, 1932.
Dear Sir,-
In connection with the organization of the work of the radio broadcasting commission, it is becoming urgently important that the services of a director of publicity be secured as well as a director of programs. I have discussed the matter with the prime Minister, who assures me that the question is being taken up of an amendment to the act, whereby these .and other important key positions on the staff of the commission may be exempted from the provisions of the Civil Service Act. In the meantime I should be glad if your commissioners would give consideration to the temporary employment, for a period of three months, of Mr. E. C. Buchanan as director of publicity at $6,500 per annum, and Mr. E. A. Weir, at present employed with the radio

division of the Canadian National Railways, at $6,500 per annum, as director of programs and station relations.
As I indicated above, the question of the permanent appointment of the incumbents of these positions will, it is hoped, be dealt with under an amendment to the act, but in the meantime I should appreciate it if the commission could see its way clear to sanction the above temporary appointments. It is important, in view of certain commitments about to be entered into, that these appointees should enter our service by December 1st.
Yours faithfully,
Hector Charlesworth,
Chairman,
Canadian Broadcasting Commission. The Secretary,
The Civil Service Commission,
Ottawa, Ontario.

The chairman of the Canadian broadcasting commission reports that appointments to these positions are urgently required.
That report is signed by W. J. Roche as chairman and J. E. Tremblay as commissioner,
and a space is provided for the signature of the Minister of Marine. The next letter is from the chairman of the radio commission to the secretary of the Civil Service Commission. It is dated February 16, 1933, and reads:

I would call your attention to my letter of November 24 in which I asked you to give consideration to the temporary employment for a period of three months of Mr. E. C. Buchanan in connection with the public relations activities of the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Commission.
In view of the urgent necessity of the commission obtaining more publicity for the programs which we are now putting out, we would ask you to give this matter your attention in order to obtain the necessary certificate for Mr. Buchanan under section 40 of the Civil Service Act, Mr. Buchanan to be employed by our commission as director of public relations at a salary of $6,500 per annum.
It is considered that Mr. Buchanan's services should begin as and from February 15, 1933.

There you are! There we have the chairman of Canada's Radio Broadcasting Commission, himself a well known Conservative propagandist, urging with all his power the appointment of Buchanan, a government extremist, as director of public relations at twice the salary he is worth or could draw in the open market.

That is the viewpoint of the Civil Service Commission, that is the viewpoint of its secretary and it is the viewpoint of anyone who wants to build up an efficient Civil Service Commission in Canada. As I say, that letter was signed by the secretary of the Civil Service Commission. The next letter is from Mr. Hector Charlesworth to Mr. W. Foran, the secretary of the Civil Service Commission. It is dated February 23, 1933, and reads:
Dear Mr. Foran,-
I have yours of February 22nd relative to our request for the appointment of Mr. E. C. Buchanan as director of public relations.
I beg to advise you that last evening we received personal assurance from the Prime Minister that an amendment to the Radio Broadcasting Act would be submitted before the close of the session covering this as well as other matters. In accordance with the terms of your letter I therefore ask that the certificate be issued for Mr. Buchanan as from February 15th.

I shall not read further from this return. The point I wish to emphasize is that the Civil Service Commission tried to stand its ground, took the stand that it ought to take in order that it might function properly and successfully in the interests of the people of Canada, but it was prevented from carrying out its functions. It was prevented by political interference from doing what it thought it ought to have done, and that political interference came from the present government, came from the cabinet of Canada, came from the Prime Minister of this country, and because of that political interference the Civil Service Commission had to sidetrack its real functions and make appointments which should only have been made after advertisement and after competition. To my mind, Mr. Speaker, that is a very important and serious departure. If we are going to have the Prime Minister and the cabinet of this country go out and take the stand which I have shown the house was taken, I see no future for the Civil Service Commission in this country. It will be impossible for it to function as it should function, and it will become nothing more or less than a political commission. It is no wonder that we have heard argument after argument from member after member here this afternoon that the Civil Service Commission was gradually being undermined and destroyed, and it is being gradually destroyed by the government taking unto itself the making of appointments which are purely political, perhaps appointments which should not be made because of a lack of efficiency and a lack of those qualities that are necessary to give that

Radio Broadcasting Act
efficient service for which the people of Canada are paying.
I think I have made clear, Mr. Speaker, my stand and that of the party to which I belong in regard to the bill before the house, and its effect upon the efficiency of the Civil Service Commission. I hope that the government will take new ground and act differently towards the Civil Service Commission, instead of continuing to do what it has been doing for the last year or two, deliberately making it a commission that is becoming weaker and weaker every day.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If no one else is going to speak
I may say that since early this morning this house has been engaged in discussing the measure, the second reading of which I moved, and I venture to say that if anyone will take the trouble to look at Hansard he will find that all that is referable ito this measure can be contained in a very few pages. The discussion has wandered on in that way.
First of all I would like to say that the observations made by the right hon. leader of the opposition as to the undesirability of this measure being brought in at this date give expression to a sound objection. It is an objection to which I attach a great deal of importance. It arises by reason of circumstances over which the government had no control. The last member who spoke (Mr. McIntosh) referred to the fact that there was an earnest endeavour on the part of the commission to get a particular individual to act with them, and that they spoke to me, and I suggested that that could not be done unless there were amendments to the act, which is true; but I did not desire to commit myself to amendments to this act with respect to matters of that kind unless I knew something more about it than I then did. As a result of the very kind thought of the government of Great Britain we were able to ask Major Gladstone Murray to come here. After he had agreed to come, he was detained and he did not arrive here until much later than was expected. He completed a trip over Canada, not accompanied by the commission, and made an interim report on the fifth of May, which was read to the house this morning. It became apparent that in his opinion it was desirable to make certain amendments to the act, and I intimated the other day that I would introduce those amendments, but I do so reluctantly at this stage of the session. But inasmuch as it has been represented to me that it is absolutely imperative, if we are to save this commission, that action of this kind should be taken, I brought the measure to
the attention of the house yesterday and moved its second reading to-day.
Does this house desire to preserve the radio broadcasting business of Canada for the Canadian people? That is the first question. If that question is answered in the affirmative, then we must select the instrumentality of government by which we shall effect that purpose. It is not a department of government; it is a business, an industry. And in the same way that provinces select liquor commissions to transact their business, so in this instance the Dominion government believes, as shown by the statute that has been passed, that the instrumentality by which we can accomplish our purpose is a commission of three persons.
It will be observed that there is a great distinction between a department of government and a commission. A department of government, as the very words indicate, is responsible to this parliament in a narrow sense. A commission is an instrumentality set up by parliament itself to accomplish certain purposes and achieve certain ends. The liquor commission of Quebec makes no report to anyone except a report as .to its operations. It buys, it sells, it receives money, it pays out money. The liquor commission of Alberta buys and sells without reference to the government and turns its profits over to the province. The liquor commission of Ontario, I understand, although I am not so familiar with its operations, conducts its business in exactly the same way. Why is that so? Because being instrumentalities of government, government has clothed them with powers and holds them responsible for the discharge of the powers conferred upon them, and the government must accept the responsibility as between the people and the legislature. That is this case. Whether we like it or not, that is what we have tried to do. It is folly not to recognize the fact that a very persistent and determined effort is being made to destroy this commission. I do not think that hon. gentlemen opposite are desirous of assisting in its destruction. We know how this commission is looked upon by private interests outside of this country. We know exactly the powers in this country that were so disappointed because the radio committee did not report in favour of private interests controlling broadcasting in this dominion. The report that was read this afternoon by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) indicates clearly what was in the mind of that committee when, it dealt with this matter.
We have determined that we will not part with our broadcasting rights in Canada. We

have determined that at this stage of scientific development we are going to cling to those rights, but we are going to endeavour to give ,to the Canadian people some reasonable service in the way of broadcasting facilities. We have charged a license fee of two dollars. The taxpayer of this country is not responsible for the moneys expended by the radio commission.
The only persons who have an interest in that matter are those who take out their licences, and every user of a radio is supposed to have taken out a licence. That money we said last year, and we repeat this year, is money for the expenditure of which this commission should be responsible. It is money which partners in the enterprise have entrusted the commission to expend for them, and parliament has taken the necessary action to preserve this business for the Canadian people. If, Mr. Speaker, it is thought for a moment that this commission can successfully function if it has to come and report to this house in answer to a question as to whether Jane Smith was a contralto or a soprano, or whether she sang on a certain night, and what she was paid-it must be a failure inevitably and positively. There can be no doubt about it. Every thoughtful man knows it, every observer knows it; but that is the criticism made by the opposition and private interests. We may be asked, "What is the name of the announcer at station so and so; where was he bom; what size boots does he wear?" We may be asked, "Did Jane Smith, or somebody else, come from New York to sing?" If that sort of thing is to continue I say to this House of Commons this afternoon: Gentlemen, you have destroyed the thing you desired to protect. That is as certain as anything in the world, and there is no thoughtful member of the house who does not realize it.
In the face of that fact we have one great illustration, the British Broadcasting Corporation. Sir John Reith became responsible as chairman of it, and the gentleman chosen largely to direct its activities was an Ontario bom Canadian., and in him I think most of us feel a great sense of pride. May I say incidentally that if hon. members are disposed to discuss the question of salaries I advise them to consider the salary paid by the British Broadcasting Corporation to that gentleman, as compared with the salaries we pay in this country. I mention that in passing only. The British Broadcasting Corporation have had a wide experience; they have had a successful experience. They have dealt with technical problems of the first magnitude. They have dealt with the tastes, the desires and the

wishes of their clientele, those people who own licences and radios throughout the kingdom, and they have established a great reputation.
But think of our position in this country. I am bound to say the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) put it fairly, as did the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler). Look at our position. We live in the northern half of the Amerioan continent. Anyone who knows anything about the theory of radio broadcasting knows that the strength and the power of a station to transmit and send through the air the human voice so that it may be collected again and be made to sound like the human voice, is a matter purely technical in its nature. So greatly has science advanced that it has become simply a question of being able to determine with great exactness the strength and power necessary to project the human voice along certain channels to a given point where it is picked up and repeated, just as we hear it over the receiving instruments in our homes.
Let us put the position fairly. There are in the United States a large number of very powerful stations. If there is no arrangement made internationally between this country and the United States it follows, inevitably, that any stations we put up of lesser power will be choked by the confusion which will result from projections by high powered stations of the vibrations of the voice through the ether, as they say,-and now they say there is no ether-we will say through space, for the purpose of having the voice collected at another point. This confusion is inevitable, unless arrangements are made between countries. We have an international agreement.
I was rather hurt when I heard one hon. member state that the Minister, of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) had had a good holiday at Madrid. Shall Canada be represented in international radio conferences? The Minister of Marine did not desire to make that long trip to Madrid at that time of year, strange as it may sound to the gentleman who made that observation in the house to-day. When he reached there, due to his mastery of both English and French, he, with his technical advisers, was able to take a very leading part in the transactions of the conference, a matter of gratification to most Canadians. He had with him a highly trained technician. I have not had the pleasure of knowing Colonel Steel for many years. I met him a couple of years ago, or more. But I do know this, that in other countries he is spoken of as one of t'he foremost technicians known. I thought we were exceedingly fortunate in getting him

for the technical position. I would not say that his training fitted him to deal with public relations, but for technical purposes he is qualified. At Madrid he was able to render great service.
In the meantime we desired to set up this commission. I desired to secure his services. He could not get away from Madrid. I cabled the minister, and although the minister found it difficult to get away, finally he came. Colonel Steel stopped in England, saw the English authorities who gave him full facilities with respect to the stations they had, and the great station they were building. The officials gave him every possible facility. I saw him myself, in December, in England. He was anxious to get back here and to obtain information as to the working of our own system. He came back to Canada.
The commission was organized under the chairmanship of Mr. Charlesworth. I have heard much criticism of Mr. Charlesworth to-day. I am not in a position to speak with any degree of authority with respect to Mr. Charlesworth, due to the fact that I did not (know him intimately. I never have known him intimately. I was advised by friends who had wide knowledge of the matter-not of one political party

but to whom I had made application for information, that Mr. Charlesworth was, first, a man of letters and of wide culture, a sound critic and would understand something of the tastes of the Canadian people, that he had travelled throughout Canada and would be able admirably to direct the operations of such a commission.
An objection has been made so often in this chamber that it does not need repeating, concerning the appointment of Mr. Maher from Quebec. But those who know anything about what he has done since he has been appointed all agree he has acquitted himself admirably, and is a first rate official in every respect. I will say this, frankly,-I said it before, and I say it now-it is one of those unfortunate circumstances that he had been actively interested in political matters before he was appointed. That may make some of my friends opposite, as the hon. member for North Waterloo said, look upon him with suspicion. But I will challenge any hon. member of this house to say or to show that in the conduct of the duties and obligations of his position he has in any sense been political in any way, Shape or form. I say that very frankly, because I think if ever a man desired earnestly to make for himself a reputation, and a reputation of which he might be proud, it is Mr. Maher.
There is your commission,

your technician, your chairman and your vice-chairman. There you have the problem, with this great country to the south with 120,000,000 people, and with all its powerful stations. You know the network of them,-the one outside of New York city, the very powerful one at Schenectady, the one at Cincinnati, then down the western coast, and as far as Texas. We have the one across the Texas boundary with strength sufficient to produce interference even in this country. There is your situation.
I say, sir, to my friends in this house that before this commission was organized, and there was no control of the national business of broadcasting, we were rapidly heading for chaos. Why? Because with the confusion of wave lengths, channels, and conditions incident to the very powerful stations just across an imaginary line, you have a situation which, unless it is taken up and dealt with firmly will mean what the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) described,-not only chaos, but a condition in which you are trying to repair your house and live in it at the same time. No one knows better than I, because I have endeavoured to follow this matter with care, being most anxious to preserve this broadcasting business for the Canadian people, the unpopularity for the moment of this commission. But I do ask the members of this house to be fair. I ask men who have had experience in business to be fair. We have been told this afternoon that there is no need of this house having experts about anything, therefore I know I am speaking to men who are experts in business as well as other matters -knowing that as I do, I ask any hon. member of this house whether he thinks it is quite fair, remembering that Colonel Steel did not get back from Madrid until the first part of this year, to launch such a campaign of attack against this commission as we have had here to-day? Would you think it fair in regard to any business that you were asked to reorganize? Which one of us asked to reorganize a business would make attacks at the end of a few months on the position in which the business then stood? I have watched this thing with care, and I propose to do so because I am tremendously interested in its success; for if it fails the whole principle of the people owning this great facility will have been destroyed. Colonel Steel assured me that undoubtedly in connection with our international agreements, in connection with working them out, in connection with the fact that we are trying to follow an orderly course prescribed by international agreement to bring

a measure of order out of chaos-and I use that word in no way offensively or critically- the discharge of that duty would take time. In the report of the committee three to five years was mentioned, but in less than that number of months we have this attack launched in the terms in which it has been made to-day against this commission. I ask, Mr. Speaker, if the members of this house will not be a little fairer in dealing with this problem-because it is a problem. We have selected an instrumentality, and having selected that instrumentality let us give it a chance.
Now I come to the first point, the question of staff and personnel. Is it the desire of this house that the broadcasting commission should be required in the first instance to go to the Civil Service Commission to ask whether or not they may employ this or that band, this or that orchestra, this or that artist? That is the very negation of the principles and purpose for which this commission came into being.

In course of time I am satisfied that these difficulties will be ironed out and the obstacles removed to which reference was to be made. I have this point to make to the hon. member for Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset). I realize that last year a committee made a report to this house, which with the exception of a single member was accepted by all. It is my most earnest desire that the radio business should come back to that position where as one voice we speak our determination to maintain it as a national undertaking. I am certain we can do it only by bringing about a common understanding and an earnest desire to have success follow the efforts of those to whom we have entrusted this work. I therefore suggest that the house pass this bill; that it limit its operation to the first of July, 1934, that we then call into being at the next session a committee to which this whole matter may be referred, in order that the house once more may speak for the whole nation and not for any party with respect to a matter of this kind. I confess that I felt somewhat distressed this afternoon to find all the opposition coming from my hon. friends across the gangway. I cannot think that that is in the interests of this great national undertaking.
Hear, hear.

No words that I can use would exaggerate what I conceive to be the importance of this matter in relation to the body politic. I look upon it as one of the foremost means of education that the world has ever known, and I believe we must not permit it to be destroyed either by political differences or by the insidious efforts of private interests to destroy public ownership of this utility.
I might have said this before had I made any remarks when the motion was made for the second reading of the bill; the delay is excused only by the reasons I have given. I believe it would have been preferable to send this bill to a committee so that it might have had an opportunity of again hearing Major Gladstone Murray's explanations as to why he came to the conclusions he did 53719-3095

But this I say in no too critical sense: When any government, after much solicitation, inconveniences itself as well as its instrumentality, the British Broadcasting Corporation, to secure the loan of one of our own distinguished sons, I think it is a little lacking in the courtesy that should be extended to him to have the criticisms and statements made that we heard in this house with respect to that gentleman. I say that to my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), whose remarks were wholly unworthy of him, I think, on an occasion such as this.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the bill should be given second reading, and in reply to the suggestion of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) that it should be dropped I suggest that a clause be added providing that it shall expire on the first day of July, 1934. A committee will be appointed in due course to consider the matters here dealt with, and I cannot conceive that under those circumstances any great injury will be done to the Civil Service Commission or any other cause to which reference has been made to-day. During the interim we will provide an opportunity for those charged with the responsibility to discharge those obligations which the statute places upon them in the manner they desire, which will reflect credit upon themselves, I am sure, and give satisfaction to the Canadian people. Long before this commission came into being there were complaints with regard to radio reception in this city; it is well known that there are difficulties in the way of radio reception at particular points. All these problems are being studied, and I trust that they will be overcome. I hope we will sufficiently realize the importance of this matter not to confine our criticisms to purely political lines, but that an earnest effort will be made to promote the well being of radio broadcasting as a public utility in this dominion.

No. Mr. Chairman. I want to talk on it. It is bad enough to have my hearing denied without being imposed upon. I think I have a right to be heard. I haven't had a word to-day at all. I did not intend to speak to-day but I do want to say a few words on section 1.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
On section 2-Powers of commission.

Mr. Chairman, I
do not rise to speak as one who knows very much about radio. We had one in our house on the farm until we became too poor to
Radio Broadcasting Act

keep it in batteries. It is there now just to look at. It may not be much of an ornament, but it is a reminder of better days. Maybe we will be able to get batteries for it when conditions improve. But it does not require much knowledge of radio to be able to make some observations on section 2 of this bill.
At this point I should like to be permitted to indicate the tendency of the government's activities. So far as I can discern them, they are all in the direction of getting all the national services in their own hands-for tvhat purpose, we can only conjecture. In order to amplify my remarks in regard to this particular section, may I say that it would seem that they are providing for all appointments to be made outside the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission, thereby making the radio commission a political institution, if they so desire.
I managed to hear some of the remarks of the Prime Minister and they were deeply interesting to me. Not knowing much about radio, it was news to me to learn of the ease with which powerful stations can be established in the United States and drive less powerful stations in Canada off the map. If they can be established there, powerful stations could be established in this country that would drown out everybody else.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And cost a lot of money.

Yes, it would take a lot of power, and it would cost a lot of money, but when politics is at stake, a little power here or there does not amount to much to a millionaire government when it comes to getting a monopoly of the air. But if this can be done in the United States, if their powerful stations drown us out and jam our instruments, what is to hinder the government of Canada, with all the power it will have with this radio system, with the government appointed commission all of whom are friends of the government-what is to hinder this government establishing a powerful radio station and putting all their opponents off the map?

We never thought of
that.
Perhaps I am displaying ignorance about radio, but I do not know that I am. I am not displaying any ignorance as to the capacity of governments to do this kind of thing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: You should know.

That is exactly
what was done by the government previous to 1893 in their election act provisions; I went 
through it, and I know. I do not need to be told; it is not something I have forgotten or that I have got from somebody else; it is something I know from practical experience as having been directed against myself.
May I illustrate right now some evidence of this? May I show what is going on now? I do not wish to make any assertions concerning the redistribution bill, but may I point out by way of illustration, to give emphasis to my remarks about radio, that the government is bringing down a redistribution bill which is the most ingenious and diabolical ever conceived by either man or devil.
Order.

That is true. If
a government will hobble me and behead me, -I am just talking about myself as an illustration-mutilate me and crucify me under one bill, for absolutely political reasons, why can they not do it-
I ask the hon. member to keep in order, and to speak to the section before the committee.
Oh, oh.
