speechtext: Respect for age is something, but this nonsense should stop..
The Prime Minister does not need to look cross.
He says it is nonsense.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is a shame, that is all.

First there is redistribution, with our heads already in the noose; all you have to do is pull the rope. Is that not so? The axe is suspended right over our heads. I am showing the tendencies of this government to prepare all along the line for an election, so that they may hobble, hamstring and cripple their opponents as much as possible, thereby making them relatively impotent for that great battle. They are winning as many outposts as possible in advance, tha't is what they are doing. Nobody can fool me on the signs of the political times. If the government does not like my exposing them, it is not my fault. It is my business to expose them, and to warn the people of what is happening. They tried out, in a small way, the political stunt on the penitentiary bill to grab off all appointments from the Civil Service Commission. The government is getting a fine stand-in with the big fellows in the militia. I know what can be done through the police-I know, mighty well. We have not had mounted police in the west for over fifty years without our knowing that if you have a political appointee at the head, considerable political work can be done through him.

You are talking from
experience, are you?

Theory, do you say? I say when you have your own or your party's hide ripped asunder by it, it is not a theory. Now we will get back to the bill. I have given some illustrations to show what is going on. After the franchise being won by our
forefathers a hundred or more years ago, partly through bloodshed, I object to hon. gentlemen opposite swiping it from me in broad daylight by any device, without a word of protest.
Oh, oh.

You do not need to laugh. The man who laughs at that only displays his own ignorance, and he does not know anything about the political history of Canada, modern or remote.
Now, about this bill-but by the way, I have another illustration, the Canadian National Railways. What about them? We know about the legislation that has just passed-and all these things have happened in the last ten days. We know about the board of trustees, all appointees of the government. Did anybody ever hear of words being passed from the upper fellow, the man at the top, down all along the line, as to what the men at the bottom should do at election time? Anybody who has not heard of that should not be sitting in this chamber. He is too innocent to be living this side of the Jordan. There are three or four illustrations bearing directly on the political possibilities of this bill. Now my good friend the Prime Minister says it is nonsense for me to suggest-he himself put the thought in my mind-what could be done by these powerful radio stations. Did anyone in this house ever hear a more powerful, a more effective orator over the radio than my right lion, friend? I heard him in 1930 and I never heard his equal on the radio in my life. A clear, ringing voice-yes, I see he appreciates that-a clear, resonant voice, a wide vocabulary; he never needs to hesitate a moment for a word, as I have to, unfortunately. And he carried conviction because there was an element of sincerity in his voice that would deceive even the very elect. Put two or three speakers like that on a government radio system, with a powerful station that will jam off everyone else, and goodbye opponents-particularly if it is assisted by this gerrymandering bill already referred to if it is carried out; I do not know whether it will be or not. But there is only one thing lacking for a complete hamstringing and emasculating of the electors of Canada at the next general election and disfranchising them not by thousands but by hundreds of thousands, that is an election act such as we had in 1895 or that under the War Time Elections Act when every disputed ballot was put in an envelope and you had to prove at great expense that it was any particular candidate's vote. There is not one candidate in
Radio Broadcasting Act

fifty who is wealthy enough to stand the resultant expense. That is all that is lacking to make the government's election plans complete.
You will observe from my remarks that I do not know much about radio but I know a whole lot about Tories. I should know a lot about Tory tactics prior to elections; forewarned by past experience is forearmed, and I want to warn not only this house but the country at large what our good friends over there are preparing for us. What a commentary i't is on the lack of confidence they have in themselves or the electors when they have to resort to these devices to fool the people and try to ward off the verdict against them that is bound to come if things are permitted to run their natural course.

Mr. Chairman, I had the misfortune of being called out of the chamber this afternoon and could not follow the speech of my right hon. friend. But fortunately I came back in time to receive his reprimand, I might even say his castigation, for having dared to say that Mr. Murray had been lecturing parliament in that interim report which was read this morning.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: And that he should be sent home.

I do not remember having said that, but if I did not say it then I say it to-night. I quite agree with my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) ; my right hon. friend seems to be pleased or grateful for having had the loan of this gentleman, but I say we have too many loans of this kind. The Finance minister was saying the other day that we are still a borrowing nation; I knew that as regards finance, but I do not think we should borrow gentlemen from England o-r elsewhere to come and tell Canadians what they should do with their own national problems.
Mr. HACIvETT: He is a Canadian.

He is not living in Canada now.
Mr. HACIvETT: He has been absent a short time.

Is it lacking in courtesy to resent its being said to members of this parliament that parliament should not have control in this matter, that, according to this gentleman, parliament is not qualified for that sort of work? Is it lacking in courtesy to resent that? I think my right hon. friend
wrong; his criticism should be directed the (Mr. Motherwell.]
other way. Moreover he should defend parliament and the members of the house against the language of the chairman of his radio board, who has said somewhere that any man who thinks that the radio commission is not doing what should be done is either a liar or a fool.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Has the hon. gentleman
authority for that Statement?
I saw it in the newspapers.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have received no evidence of it, but in view of what was said here I am writing to ask what wias actually said.

I am pleased that my
right hon. friend will try to remedy grievances of members of the house, and not resent too much the defence we have to put up against the reflections of this gentleman and others who are borrowed from elsewhere to come and tell us how to solve the problems of Canada.
There is one matter, however, as to which I agree with my right hon. friend; it is deplorable that there is no longer unanimity in this house-and I might say elsewhere-with regard to radio affairs in Canada. But whose fault is that? I have said that I have no confidence in the present commission, and I believe that the majority of the Canadian people have no confidence in it. Who is responsible for that? I am not responsible. I think the appointments to the commission were unfortunate. I think that what has happened since the commission has been appointed also is unfortunate, and that is the real cause of the unpopularity of that board with the 'Canadian people at the present time. My hon. friends the Minister of Marine and the Solicitor General have replied to me on the basis of statements I did not make, but I wish to refer to one argument of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine. I criticized, and I still criticize, the issuing of a licence to a newspaper in Montreal for radio broadcasting a month after the appointment of the commission, and two days before they were sworn in, without the matter being submitted to the commission. The very fact that this has been done is an indication that the government did not keep faith with the house and wanted to evade the provisions of the Radio Broadcasting Act. Under that act, section 8, it is the duty of the commission to determine the number, location and power

Radio Broadcasting Act
of stations required in Canada. And by subsection (c):
The commission may make recommendations to the minister with regard to the issue, suspension or cancellation of private broadcasting licences, and notwithstanding anything contained in the Radiotelegraph Act or regulations, the minister may issue, suspend, or cancel such licences.
What I more particularly object to is not the issuing of the licence to that newspaper, had it been done in the regular way by the commission or upon the recommendation of the commission. What I object to is that the licence was issued between the appointment of the commission and the swearing in of its members. My horn, friend the Minister of Marine said: well, it is a Conservative newspaper and it is a good thing that both parties have their stations. Surely this house would not subscribe to such a policy, that there should be an allotment of broadcasting stations in Canada on political lines, so many for the Conservatives, so many for the Liberals. The house never contemplated that when we adopted tire Radio Broadcasting Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
In your time it was
only the Liberals.

Never. What Liberal
station ever did that?

La Presse, the Toronto
Star and others.

I never understood La
Presse to be a Liberal newspaper. Let me say that at election times, and at other times as well, I have heard speeches delivered by hon. gentlemen opposite over the La Presse station. That never has been considered a Liberal station. From La Patrie I think almost every day we have talks by gentlemen who call themselves Labour-Conservatives or others who represent an organization called the Federation of Labour, which is merely a Tory association, as all hon. gentlemen opposite know. I still say, Mr. Chairman, that to divide the licences in Canada on political lines, so many to one party and so many to another, is a wrong principle that cannot be accepted or subscribed to by this house.
There was another thing said toy hon. gentlemen opposite in defence of this act; they say that Toronto had four broadcasting stations and it was not right that Montreal should have only two. What advantage is there in having so many broadcasting stations? It merely brings about confusion. I do not think it is of any benefit to the community that there should be several small stations; I do not think there should be a
competition as between Toronto and Montreal or Vancouver and Winnipeg as to the number of stations in each city. Rather I think good service and quality should be looked for in the organization of radio broadcasting.
My hon. friend from Dorchester, who was one of the members of the committee last year, said that committee had reported that stations of less than one hundred watts should not come under the commission. Whatever may have been contained in the report of that committee it is the law which governs in the matter, and there is nothing in the broadcasting act accepting the report of the committee in this regard; all stations come under the radio commission.
There is another point to which I should like to direct attention. Some hon. member who discussed this question to-day praised himself and the house for having had the support of the radio league in this matter, and the name of Mr. Graham Spry was mentioned in this connection. I knew the radio league had suggested that instead of a board appointed by the government and paid for its services there should be a sort of honorary board on which all sections of the country and of the community would be represented by men who would be willing to serve without expense to the country, and the real executive work should be entrusted to a general manager. That was the program suggested by the radio league. In the April 27th issue of the Weekly Sun, which is edited by Mr. Graham Spry, who was the president of the league, I see an article headed "The Radio Commission". I am not going to read it all, but here is part of what Mr. Spry says:
The Canadian Radio League proposal, first advanced in detail in the Queen's Quarterly, January, 1931, provided for a voluntary commission to which a competent and experienced general manager would be responsible for the practical details of administering broadcasting. In this way, the formulation ot policy would have been separated from its administration, as in the case of a company with its board of directors and its general manager and staff. There would have been the additional advantage that the voluntary board, selected by consultation between the three parties, would have represented different parts of Canada, would have been independent of partisan interest, and in a position to resist partisan pressure. This is the British scheme, and the British board, rather than the government, are held responsible for administration, thereby saving the government from criticism for the acts of its semi-autonomous commission.
The government of Canada, however, saw fit to establish a commission that combined the formulation of policy with its administration; then it appointed a commission, one of whose members was a former Conservative organizer. Subsequent acts and appointments of the com-
Radio Broadcasting Act

mission, rightly or wrongly, were taken by the public and the opposition parties to be partisan. The radio commission, therefore, became subject to political pressure and party criticism.
And so on. I think there was much to commend itself in the proposal of the radio league; certainly we would have avoided the situation in which we find ourselves to-day. My right hon. friend does not like it; no one likes it. We all supported the idea of nationalizing the radio, of public ownership; there was never such unanimity in the house as when the bill was made law during the last session of parliament. We were told by the right hon. gentleman that politics would not enter into appointments to the board which was to be created to administer radio affairs, but unfortunately we think faith has not been kept so far as that promise and that pledge are concerned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We say that politics has not entered into it.

I cannot understand my right hon. friend when he says that politics did not enter, when he has put there to represent a large section of the community a man who not only was his candidate in the last election but who has been the organizer of his party for three or four elections. So far as I am concerned I do not believe that man can administer radio affairs in my district impartially. I do not trust the radio commission, as it is now constituted, for the next general election or for any other matter in my district. It is a sad condition in which to find myself; I should prefer to have confidence in that board. I agree with my right hon. friend that confidence is necessary for the success of radio broadcasting in Canada, but if confidence is lacking we are not responsible; the government is responsible, and I am sorry to say that until that condition is corrected it will be impossible for the people of Canada to get along well with the board which is in control of radio broadcasting, and until that condition is created we shall not have success or harmony.
Mr. LaVERGNE (Translation): Mr. Chairman, the 'hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) lias no objection to an exclusively conservative or liberal station, and he is quite right; however, there are people who are in a more unfortunate position than that; some have no station. I wish to apprise the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) of what happened to me. As Coppee would say: My story, gentlemen on the bench will be brief. Once, for my good or ill fortune, I delivered a speech, at Montmagny, on the Imperial

economic agreements, and some enthusiastic person-there are always some-requested me to repeat it in Quebec. During two months, I received from station CHRC dilatory replies, followed by an absolute refusal; they gave no excuse or reason. I wish to inquire from the hon Minister of Marine, whether persons holding government licences to operate broadcasting stations have a right to refuse a private individual the use of their station, providing he does not offend public decency or order-I felt that I had offended neither the one nor the other-and providing that, in requesting the use of the station for half an hour, he gives them sufficient notice, such as a week, two weeks or even two months. Mr. LaVERGNE (Translation):	It was

speechtext:

As soon as I get a reply, I shall be pleased to get in touch with my hon. friend.
Mr. LaVERGNE (Translation): That is what I wished to know. I have no reproach to make to the hon. Minister. I am aware that the Radio Commission is practically independent. I would think that having obtained a franchise from the people, they are there to cater to the public, therefore, the Radio Commission should have over these stations a more efficient and complete control. If not, the commission would not serve the purpose for which it was created.
A broadcasting station-the hon. Minister stated-is owned by an independent corporation, and I understand, aocording to his remarks, that a station has absolute control of its program and the broadcasting hours placed at the disposal of the public.

Mr. LaVERGNE (Translation): In this case, it might, perhaps, be necessary to amend the Radio Broadcasting Act, in this respect.
I am very much of the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Quebec East, because in fact, that might lead to tyranny or partiality and this would totally fall short of the aim which we had in view when creating the commission. The radio broadcasting stations are established to cater to the public, the moment they observe our constitution, our laws-

Peace and good order.

preferences. I, for one, strongly criticize the CHRC station of Quebec, not because it affects me but because it affects others. I
[Mr LaVergne.]
often had the occasion of broadcasting my speeches, speaking both in front and behind the broadcasting mouthpiece. What does one speec-h more or less-I would gladly dispense making them. I wish, sir, to support the attitude taken by the hon. member for Montmagny. If the government has full control of radio in Canada, then the commission, the authorities in charge must see that everybody has fair play, so far as radio service is concerned. The moment that a public man does not express subversive views against public order or peace, I think he is entitled to obtain from radio stations, holding a government licence and under the control of the commission, that his speech or utterances be broadcasted by Canadian public Stations. The reason we established government control over radio, was so that everybody would be dealt fairly and justly, and I entirely agree with the hon. member for Montmagny in his remarks to the house.

The hon. member for Quebec East has told the house that the radio commission does not possess his confidence.
I think it rather unfortunate that a body occupying as important a post as that confided to this commission should, before it has really entered upon its duties, be accused by a man of the high position of the former Minister of justice of being entirely unworthy of the confidence of the country, and I think also it is extremely unfortunate that no allegation is made in support of the charge. It is true that the hon. gentleman singled out for his own personal charge the vice-president, and forsooth he said, "I cannot have any confidence in this man nor can anyone else have confidence in him because-heinous offence- he was on some occasion a Conservative candidate."
The only reason.

He goes further and says that this man has added to the crime by having been a Conservative organizer. I believe that the hon. gentleman is accurate in stating as a fact that the vice-president of the commission did at some time have something to do with politics. I should hate to think however that every member of this chamber is unfitted for any honourable post

Radio Broadcasting Act
because at some time he had sought and been found worthy of the confidence of the electorate of some constituency. I consider it most unfortunate that a distinguished member of this chamber should wish to point to every man in this house and say that because he has at some time been a partisan he is unworthy of high office. If he is going to apply that rule to this and other countries, what esteem can he have for the bench, what esteem can he have for the incumbent of any office that is worth holding?-because in democratic countries positions of high trust are invariably given to those who seek, and show themselves worthy of, the confidence of the people. I reiterate therefore that to say, without substantiating the statement, without bringing forth anything to justify such a charge, that this body which has recently come into office is unworthy of public confidence, designates, I fear, a type of mind and a partisanship which detract from the value of the judgment uttered in those words of condemnation. The hon. member says that Bill Murray should go home- and I speak of Bill Murray because he was at McGill with me, a boy from British Columbia, an active, energetic lad who has made his way in the world and is welcomed not only to Canada but to other countries where expert radio advice is sought; he is called in because he is supposed to know more about the technique of radio development than anyone else. When the hon. member refers to that gentleman as a stranger, and harks back to .that cry that is sometimes heard in the back ranges, that he is a foreigner-
I never said that. Be fair; I never said that.
I am perfectly willing to retract.
You are carried away by your own eloquence.
Take your medicine.
The hon. gentleman said that we did not require any assistance or guidance from outside.
That is not saying he is a foreigner.

If this government has fallen into that evil habit it has only fallen a victim to the bad example set by its predecessor. I will ask hon. gentlemen opposite where they went to get that lamented man who recently passed from us and who for some years headed our national railway system. Where did he come from? Then, if I remember well, there was a gentleman who came, not from Vancouver, not from
Montreal or Toronto, a gentleman who had something to do with the investigation of conditions in the maritimes and whose name I believe was Sir Andrew Rae Duncan. Where did he come from? Who summoned him here from Scotland? If I remember well, there was also a report made with regard to the Hudson Bay terminal, a vast and costly report which was made by a most skilled and able man. He did not come from Toronto or Montreal, he came from England; his name was Sir Frederick Palmer.
I think that was a mistake.

It may have been a mistake but I am willing to do the hon. gentleman and his friends justice by saying that they went where they thought they were able to get the best man they could. Now that is all that this government has done. Let us therefore be fair to the radio commission and realize that it is trying to become something of which we shall all be proud. Let us give it a fair chance.

I will not detain the committee very long, but I want to say a few words with respect to this small station in Quebec which seems to have incurred the displeasure of my hon. friend from Montmagny A few minutes ago my hon. friend from Quebec East, when speaking about the radio broadcasting commission, reproached me for having quoted the report which was made last year by the committee that sat on radio broadcasting matters. I shall quote not only the report of the radio committee but also the law. I refer my hon. friend to chapter 51 of the statutes of 1932. Subsection (g) of section 8 of the act reads:
The commission may, subject to the approval of the minister, assist and encourage the construction of small private stations.
But it is known that these small private stations of 100 watts and under remain the property of the owners. They may not be taken into the national scheme of radio broadcasting and will not be subject to the control of the Minister of Marine or the broadcasting commission except so far as programs and licences are concerned. It is a well known fact that the two small stations in Quebec city have not been taken over by the commission. In fact, no station in Canada has been taken over to form part of the national scheme of radio broadcasting. The commission contends that they cannot do this unless the law is changed.
I come now to the speech of the hon. member for Montmagny. He does not seem to

like station CHRC, but I do not think this station can be accused of narrow partisanship. I think that is demonstrated by the fact that the hon. member for Quebec East broadcast a speech over that station about a month ago. This was the speech which the hon. member for Montmagny referred to as being wonderful. I will call it a seditious speech. I think one is entitled to his own views in this regard. The hon. member for Montmagny may have his own views, the hon. member for Quebec East may have his and I may have mine. I think it was absolutely unfair to insinuate that that station has been unfair or unjust to any particular party. There happened to be some Conservatives acting as directors of this company, but I do not think that that would be sufficient to prove that the company was unfair. My hon. friend saw fit to overlook Mr. Vandry's station and broadcast over CHRC. That is his business.

I did not refer to any

The latter would have been much pleased to broadcast my hon. friend's speech. I think it is absolutely unfair to insinuate that station CHRC in Quebec city has been playing politics. Mr. LaVERGNE : Mr. Chairman, I had no intention of treading on the corns of the hon. member for Dorchester; I am exceedingly sorry if he thinks I have done so, because I did not want to arouse his ire. However, I thank him personally although I do not know whether he has done such a good service for the Minister of Marine. My quarrel with station CHRC was settled absolutely and I was satisfied with the explanations given by the Minister of Marine. I understand he was not to blame and I have no quarrel with him. However, I thought that I should put this matter before the committee as in my opinion the situation created was absolutely unfair. In saying that I do not refer to my own personal feeling. When the hon. member for Dorchester has been in parliament as long as I have he will know that it is more of a pleasure than a sorrow to put speeches on the shelf. Apparently the hon. member is acting as an advocate for station CHRC and I must tell him that he seems to be better informed about that station than the minister. He accuses me of having attacked the vice-president of the commission, but I did not do anything of the kind. The hon. member for Quebec East asked me if he was an owner of that station before his appointment and I simply answered "yes". Whether or not he is now an owner, I do not know, but I suppose he is not.
I may say to the hon. member for Dorchester that in this affair station CHRC acted without courtesy, without honesty and without courage. For two months they gave me dilatory answers. They were going to be paid and paid with the money of good friends of the hon. member for Dorchester. These people were anxious to have the speech which had been given in Montmagny broadcast in Quebec, and they were willing to pay the station. The action of this station constituted a slur either on the Conservative party or on myself. If it was only on myself, I am none the worse off; I can stand these things, but I think they have acted most unfairly. This is a public utility, to serve the public, and if

Radio Broadcasting Act
no one had been concerned but myself I would not have mentioned the matter. They have been granted a franchise and 1 claim that they are there to serve the public.
If they have a right to refuse to serve the public then it is time the law was changed. They are not there to gratify their affections or their hatreds. They are there to put that station to the service of the public of Canada, that and nothing else, and if the law does not give the commission those powers, the law should be amended. If the law does give the commission those powers, that station should be reprimanded immediately because certainly we should be missing the aim in nationalizing radio if we allowed it to become a tool in the hands of those with influence or money enough to buy or rent a station. I do not care how many stations there are, and I do not care whether it is Liberals or Conservatives or Tories or Grits or anybody else that runs them; that is a matter of indifference to me, but I say that the people of this country have a right to the radio when they wish to hear it, and nobody can make me believe that station CHRC did not have half an hour to give to the hon. member for Montmagny, especially when people have told me that they received permission to broadcast for a whole hour the next day on only one day's notice. I have no hatred or love for that particular station; I am quite indifferent; I do not know who owns it, but I want to know who owns it if it is going to continue to be operated in that way. I want to know who got the licence and through what influence, and I want to see that they do not get a licence next year if they do not act differently.

If I may presume,
Mr. Chairman, to talk a second time before the ninth hour is up on a subject I do not know a great deal about, I should like to take just five or ten minutes more-and do no.t be too harsh, Mr. Chairman, on my homely illustrations because that is the way I talk.
While I do not know much about radio I should know a lot, without presumption, about Tory-o, and that is what I am talking about, if I may; and I think the chairman is going ,to let me. I should like to give another illustration of what can be done by a government that wants to do it, and apparently this is that kind of government. I want to point out how easy it is for the government to do it, and I am going to tell the Minister that I had it worked on me once 53719-310
not by means of the radio but by monopolizing the press for advertising purposes. I will tell that story first.
When I ran a federal election campaign against a Progressive candidate for the first time in 1919 in Assiniboia in southern Saskatchewan, I found w'hen I got into the constituency that every square inch of advertising space had been taken up in advance right through the election by my enterprising friends then called the Progressives. Imagine the helplessness of one going into a contest like that! Now if our innocent friends the Progressives will do that towards a brother farmer opponent, what won't the less innocent gentlemen now occupying the treasury benches do towards an opponent by means of the radio? The hon. member for Dorchester has talked about engaging a period of time on the air over a certain radio line or wave or whatever is the technical term, but we might find that the Liberals could not get on the air for six months to come. This government will know when an election is coming on six or four or two months before the writs are issued, and .they can have every wave and everything else that goes with it engaged right through the election.
They will have a wave of public opinion.

Yes, over the left.
I know what my friends the Progressives worked on me in Assiniboia. I am not unduly suspicious when I suggest that the government might engage the radio in advance right through the election. A man would be worse than a fool who, having been burnt once, did not fight shy of fire a second time. So I say that I am not unduly suspicious. I am taking things as I find them and as 7 have found them for a half century, and they have not changed very much for the better during the last two or three years.
Here is something I cannot get over. I do not want to be too much at loggerheads with the Prime Minister, but he interjected a little time ago that what I was saying was nonsense. Well, let us see if what he was saying was not nonsense and actual bunk, and it is my business to debunk the right hon. gentleman. This radio commission had its foundations laid on party appointments. This commission is admittedly Conservative, and I am not finding fault with that as such. But good as it may be, and I know nothing about the gentlemen composing it, although I hear the chairman well spoken of-I understand that for a long number of years he was editor of Toronto Saturday Night, which I read occasionally because I rather like to

Radio Broadcasting Act

read it and find out what my opponents are saying. The foundations of the commission, then are admittedly Conservative and political; and how can you conceive that anything with a strictly Conservative foundation will be anything but Conservative? In other words, how can the superstructure be anything but political when the foundation is absolutely political? Is there a cackle over there? Did my hon. friends never hear about the principle of like begetting like? If the root be bad, what will the branches be? Unless something better is grafted on to the old root, the branches will be the same as the root; so I say that what the Prime Minister said about our criticisms was not only nonsense but it was absolutely asinine, the biggest bunk that I ever heard-to say that the foundation could be one thing and the superstructure something else absolutely opposite-neutral, non-political, with a Tory foundation. In saying that I do not want to be supercritical about the gentleman who occupies the position of chairman. The government has chosen that course, and it must not now pretend to be astonished because we expect the superstructure to be no better than the foundation. I think my conclusions are sound. I have not heard anybody get up since I spoke before and try to show that my other illustrations were not also sound. I invite anybody now to say how any government that wants to do it can be prevented from tying up the radio service in the way I have described, and just mark if it is not done.
It is only quite recently, Mr. Chairman, that the Conservative party in Canada has been noted to be friendly towards the nationalization of any utility. Everybody knows that the Canadian National was taken on by the government of that day because they did not know what else to do with it. Everybody knows that the present national radio system was taken over by this government because it was left in their lap by the preceding government. A commission had been appointed by the Liberal government to inquire into radio, headed by Sir John Aird, and the commission made a unanimous report prior to the retirement of the former government. Public sentiment was so strongly behind that report that when this government came into office it could not do otherwise than carry out the recommendations of the commission. The government made the most of it and accepted that report, and put its recommendations into operation with a magnificent speech on the general subject of nationalized air sendee by the right hon.

the Prime Minister. They did not like it particularly, because they are really only the foster parents. That is all they can claim to be of any of these great national utilities. Then why not turn the radio service to some further useful account, so that it could be used during an election? That is what they are going to do, do not make any mistake about it. They have not been slow in making use of other things, as I have ahead}"- described. The leopard, as a rule, does not change his spots, or the Ethiopian his skin, just over night. I promised to take only five minutes- six minutes, possibly-and that time has now expired. I do not believe I shall speak longer, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I frankly deplore the suggestion of the hon. member for South Perth that this commission should be under the direction or control of any minister of this or any other government. Technically, of course, I know he is not subject to that control, nor does the act give the minister any power of direction or discipline other than tihe authority vested in the governor in council to dismiss the commissioners for cause.
As a result of the castigation the commission has been getting to-night-a castigation which very frankly I think was coming to it *-I trust it will develop some tact and some character of administration in connection with broadcasting that will endear it to the people of this country, and make them have some respect for and confidence in it. I should like to see radio broadcasting so controlled by such a commission that, as in Great Britain, a debate of this kind could not and would not take place. I hope that day comes, but remember that after all the commission has succeeded in creating widespread distrust and dissatisfaction, and certainly it must mend its ways if the nationalization of radio is to be a success. I think all our comments should be confined, so far as possible, to facts; I agree with the minister in that regard. Personally I have heard all sorts of rumours. Some I have discovered to be quite untrue while others have had sufficient foundation to justify the attacks that have been made on the commission, as I said a little earlier in the evening. I do feel that hon. members of this house would be well advised to give tins converted journalist, this excellent technician and this third person, whose character and qualifications have been eloquently discussed in this house by others who know him better than I do, time to get their breath, to sense public feeling in the matter and to develop a publicly owned broadcasting system along .the lines sincerely desired by the committee last year.
I do think a mistake was made-I am free to admit it at this stage-in combining the administrative and policy-creating powers in one commission. It seemed almost impossible

to avoid doing that, though I agree that it would have been better if we had been able to accept the suggestion advanced by the president of the Canadian Radio League, which was quoted earlier this evening by the hon. member for Quebec East. In my opinion the commission failed seriously in one respect; that was in not making it perfectly clear to the public from the beginning, and not after the trouble had arisen, that the million dollars in the estimates were not and never had been taxes and were not coming out of the pockets of the taxpayers as taxes. From the commencement radio licences have been a charge on users of radio receiving sets in order that they may secure certain services in the way of a check-up on interference, closing down interruptions caused by high frequency currents, telegraph stations, leaky transformers and so on. I could testify personally to the efficiency of the Department of Marine in that aspect of their work, but during the years when the Department of Marine was carrying on that work a large surplus of money was accumulating that should have been credited directly to radio broadcasting and radio users. I understand that it went into the consolidated revenue fund and was used for general purposes. I am of the opinion that sooner or later this or some subsequent government will have to see that this money does not go into the consolidated revenue fund but is kept separate for the use of the commission and is used freely by the commission, as it is in Great Britain. Again I direct attention to that illustration. The commission should be allowed to build up its capital plant and to develop along the lines that I am sure every Canadian wants to see. Unfortunately the commission let the newspapers get away with gross misrepresentation in this connection, and I should like to direct attention particularly to the Toronto Globe. Even after that newspaper had been informed of the actual facts in connection with this sum of $1,000,000 it persisted in carrying on, in its editorial columns, a bitter and vicious attack on the ground that this was an expenditure of public money dragged out of the public by taxes. This principle should have been recognized in the very beginning.
Now for a moment or two I come to the bill itself. Section 1 is distasteful; I do not think the elimination of the operation of the Civil Service Act in the matter of appointments is wise or proper. I am willing to concede that a difficulty exists in this case, however. For example, Mr. Chairman, when the commission decides to take

Radio Broadcasting Act
over an existing radio station they will find there the general manager, the radio experts and technical men and others, probably forming a most efficient unit. I grant at once, it is unthinkable that these men should have to go back to the commission to receive what one might call eligibility as the result of an examination, and I submit that if a compromise could be reached in the matter it would be the wisest step from the point of view of all interests concerned.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that in the consideration of this aspect of the matter, the radio commission be permitted to retain those persons who are sufficiently desirable and are now employed on the staffs of any broadcasting agenicy that may be taken over by the commission, but that all new appointments of any kind, from technical men down [DOT]to stenographers, shall be made through the medium of the Civil Service Act. It is not fair to say that the Civil Service Commission is incapable of undertaking the necessary tests in connection with appointees to the radio commission. It has done it most successfully in connection with the experts of the Marine department who have been administering the Radiotelegraph Act and who were in that sendee before this commission was ever thought of. I have never heard any complaint against these technical men, and it is just a slight step from radio-telegraphy to radio broadcasting; the general principles underlying both are the same. So that I do not think it can be contended successfully that there are technical reasons Why the Civil Service Commission should not function in this case. I am satisfied that with the cooperation of the Marine department and the commission it can be made to discharge its responsibilities.
With that one criticism I have nothing further to say against the bill, but I do suggest that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Marine would be well advised to consider seriously making the Whole commission more like the British broadcasting system.
I disagree with the criticism launched at Mr. Gladstone Murray. It was my pleasure to hear him last year and I had 'the pleasure also of examining him on the committee. I met him this year again, and I think that as Canadians we can foe very proud of a fellow Canadian who has raised himself to such a high peak of efficiency in the mother country. Personally I sincerely congratulate the government on having secured the services of Mr. Murray if only for a short time. I do not think they could have secured a
better man for the work he had to do, and if his letter may have a tinge of the lecture about it, it is perhaps as well. There are many of us who need lectures on many matters.

The Labour members present in the house when the vote was taken on the second reading voted against that motion, and they did so not because they were opposed to the bill in its entirety but solely because they were opposed to the amendment in section 1. The hon. member for Bow River has put our case so well that it is not necessary for me to say anything further in that connection. I agree with everything he has said, and with this part of the question disposed of we should certainly have no objection to the rest of the bill.
May I say that neither in the house nor outside have I ever uttered a word of criticism of the commission. I think we should give the commission an opportunity to organize radio broadcasting in this country. In the short time they have been operating they have done some very good work, though possibly they have also made some mistakes. Personally I am quite willing at the moment to give them credit for the good work they have done and to overlook the mistakes they have made so far. It may be that the discussion that has taken place in this house to-day will not be lost on the commission, but in saying this I must add another word. There is another commission in this country, the Civil Service Commission, and we should also give that body an opportunity to carry on its work, which is to provide staffs for these various organizations. As a matter of fact, we are every day robbing the Civil Service Commission of any dignity it may have had, and it is not to be wondered at if it does not function as efficiently as it is supposed to do.
We are not opposed to this bill in its entirety but only to the amendment proposed in section 1, the amendment to section 4 of the aot. If some modifications were made in that regard, which would leave the bulk of the staff under the Civil Service Commission, we should have no objection to the amendment.

During his speech this morning the Minister of Marine mentioned the fact that an agreement had been reached with the United States in regard to the division of wave lengths. The agreement was made in 1932, and he said it was very profitable to Canada. Would he favour the committee with a copy of it.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
A statement was made last session to the house by the Prime Min-
Radio Broadcasting Act

ister, giving the agreement in detail. It appears in Hansard. However, I will look into the matter and if what appears in Hansard is not altogether satisfactory to my hon. friend I will try to supply the necessary information.

I think it will be generally agreed that the entire discussion on this bill has been political. On one side we hear it said that if the Liberals were entitled to stations so were the Conservatives. In my judgment that is absolutely opposed to the best interests of broadcasting in this dominion in its widest sense. If the allotment of stations is to be put on the basis of political parties, then why not go to the logical conclusion and throw the thing wide open and have complete chaos? I believe that anyone has the right to broadcast provided that in his material he keeps within the confines of the statutes of the country, because it must be remembered that radio is essentially different from any other medium of disseminating information or political agitation. It is comparatively easy to keep up a newspaper, or to rent a hall or, like the Labour party, to speak under the canopy of heaven; but broadcasting channels are naturally 'limited, and in my judgment the quickest way to destroy this great educational facility is to have it made a football of party politics. Frankly, I believe that the discussion in this house to-day has been a good thing for the nationalization of our broadcasting facilities in Canada if it has done nothing else than to clear the air and to teach members of the house and the people of the country that this institution must not be turned into a political football.
I would like to say a word or two in connection with the civil service aspect of the employees of the commission. This afternoon the Prime Minister made reference to the liquor control boards in the various provinces. I do not intend to discuss the boards in the provinces outside of my own. After all is said and done, the manner in which they approach any problem is influenced by the practical experience which we have had in relation thereto. Never since the inception of the liquor control board in Ontario have I heard of anyone but a 'Conservative being employed by that body.
Why pick on Ontario?

I live in Ontario and I do not know anything about the boards in the rest of the provinces. I am afraid that if power is given to this radio commission to have complete jurisdiction over the technical and clerical staffs, in the very nature of things the same condition will exist. Man being . what he is, this will be the natural course. If

the same policies which have been pursued in other provinces with respect to commissions absolutely divorced from government are followed by this government, there will be only one result. This question should stand far above the conflict of political parties. I believe that radio will exert an enormous force in the control of the destinies of this country. Its powers of education should be treated as almost sacred. There are many practical problems which will confront this commission and in my opinion the broadcasting of political information is one. Absolute fairness should govern in this regard and the rights and privileges of every political party, irrespective of colour or complexion, should be respected, provided its doctrine fits in with the framework, the constitution and- the laws of this country. I would not like to see happen in the next elections that which has happened in the past in my province when those who had the most money got the best facilities and naturally had the best audiences. Now that radio is being nationalized, each political party irrespective of its financial standing should have ample opportunity to make its views known to the people of this dominion.
We will not get it.
Someone says, "we will not get it," but in my judgment the people are entitled to that and they should demand it.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me what constitutes a party?
You should know as you belong to one. You had better ask that question of yourself.
You do not belong to one.

You do not know, you are just guessing. I shall support the third reading of this bill provided adequate consideration is given to the civil service aspect of the matter. I think it is within the intelligence of the government to so amend this section as to prevent the intrusion of politics into the permanent staffs of the broadcasting stations and the commission itself. There has been nothing but chaos in this country and the one to the south ever since the inception of radio, and I believe that this commission should be given ample opportunity to work out channels and wave lengths so that radio may be enjoyed by the people in every part of this dominion, not only by those in the larger centres.

There is a provision in
the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act which

Radio Broadcasting Act
had much to do with the unanimity which prevailed last year when the bill became law. Apart from providing for the appointment of a commission, the act provides that the governor in council after consultation with the provincial authorities shall appoint nine assistant commissioners, I believe one for each province. It would be the duty of these assistant commissioners to organize advisory committees in the various provinces and to act in conjunction with the private Stations. There would then be a general council convened from time to time which would be composed of the members of the central commission, the assistant commissioners and representatives of the advisory committees. This council would formulate the policies of the Commission and deal with such other matters as concerned radio broadcasting. I should like to know whether any steps have been taken towards the appointment of these assistant commissioners and the organization of these advisory committees. I believe it would be in the interests of good administration of the few if this provision was put into operation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this afternoon I explained to the committee that the technical member of the commission, because of his being detained in Madrid, was not able to carry on here until January. I explained that the commission had been endeavouring effectively to organize and to discharge its functions; that Major Murray came to this country at the request of the commission made through the government. I stated that he had made a trip through Canada unaccompanied by any member of the commission in order that it might not be said that he had formed any view which was in any sense influenced by the commission. The commission has been desirous of inspecting all radio facilities in Canada by visiting every province of the dominion but because of parliament being in session and the very unjust and unfair observations which have been made throughout Canada with respect to the million dollar appropriation, it has not been able to carry into effect its original plans. As soon as it is possible to do so, it is proposed to put the provisions of 'the statute into effect. I introduced this legislation believing as I did that the best interests of national radio would be served by the appointment of assistant commissioners. These men- would not be paid officers of the commission, and they would surround themselves with those who would give a proper bent and direction to what I might call a high national policy with respect
to radio-education, improvement in art, and all that goes with a more liberal appreciation of the outside world. I believe that that can best be effected through the methods tihat we have provided in the legislation itself, and that is why t'he provisions are there.
So far as the debate this afternoon is concerned it has to every possible extent that you can measure endeavoured to discredit the commission. The bill was taken up this morning; it is now ten o'clock, and I say that whoever looks at the record of to-day's proceedings with respect to this bill and reads what has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite with respect to this commission and its efforts to discharge its duties, will certainly not believe that those proceedings have been such as to promote the interests of national broadcasting in Canada. To criticize a commission is one thing, but to give it an opportunity t.o work is another. Some hon. members may be under the impression that the members of this commission are office boys sent out by a minister. The minister has no control over the commission, neither the Minister of Marine nor the Prime Minister. In that sense they are not errand boys or office boys nor yet servants or agents. They are a commission appointed for a purpose, and I indicated what that purpose was. The -commission present their report to the Minister of Marine and the Minister of Marine presents it to parliament, but to suggest that the commission must be called in and be -told, "You naughty boys, you must not do so and so," is to do violence to the whole underlying principle of the legislation. There has been nothing in this debate to-day to suggest what I conceived a year ago to be an earnest effort on behalf of the Canadian people to launch a great enterprise, free-shall I say?-from the carping criticism arising out of acute political differences that apparently would destroy tire commission. It is too bad. The whole debate this afternoon and all day has been sharp and acute, indicating divisions upon political party lines. Certainly every effort that a government could make was -made last year for the purpose of avoiding that very thing.
As to the observation that was made by the former Minister of Justice and by another member this afternoon, that the chairman of the commission said that any man who thought so and so was either a fool or a liar, I have not yet received any evidence of his having said i-t, but if he said it I am prepared by a minute in council to indicate in the firmest terms that that sort of talk is not worthy of members of the commission. I am ready to do that in the strongest possible
Radio Broadcasting Act

terms because I realize that the public have no right to have said to them by anyone who occupies a position in connection with a public commission words of that character.
The way in which this discussion has been carried on to-day will certainly militate against the usefulness of the commission. Its task is difficult. Why? Because, I repeat, there is opposed to it at every point the powerful private interests of the American continent who do not wish to see it succeed, and who see here the greatest experiment that ever has been, made because, in emulation of the British broadcasting system, we are endeavouring to free ourselves from all the difficulties and dangers that have followed upon private ownership. When I hear the hon. member for Melville make the attack that he did, and he was the only one, I want to say that the genesis of the whole idea of public ownership of these utilities came from Sir Adam Beck who was a member of the Conservative administration in the province of Ontario, and to-day the great hydroelectric system that has grown up in that province is the target for abuse and attack by every private interest on this continent that is connected with electrical energy and power. And, this radio is being made the butt for the same kind of attack, inspired and influenced by the same private interests on this continent.
If we are going to succeed we can succeed in only one way. Appreciating our responsibilities, we must realize what the stake is. Failure would be one more mark against public enterprise, one more failure on the part of the people to do collectively what the individual can do in private life, one more vindication of the claims of private ownership against public ownership. I am convinced beyond peradventure that if the Canadian people are to derive any benefit from radio they must continue their ownership of it as they now have it, and they can only do that not by sharply dividing the House of Commons on questions of pure partyism, by thinking in terms of Liberal or Conservative or Progressive, as I pointed out this afternoon, but by supporting the commission in its task.
I cannot conceive it possible that the former Minister of Justice was sincere in what he said this evening. I do not usually question his sincerity as he so often does mine, but I put this to him:	When a member of the
House of Commons is appointed to the bench and takes his oath of office, do I say I have no confidence in him because he opposed me in the House of Commons? I could give illustration after illustration of 
appointments to the bench from the ranks of that party during the nine years they were :n office. There was one case of a leading organizer of a great party in one province appointed to the bench, fresh from his seat in the legislature, and another case of a member of the House of Commons appointed to the bench. But would I stand in my place and say I have no confidence in the ability of that man to write honest judgments? He took the oath of office. And Mr. Maher took the oath of office that is the only oath of office you will find in the statutes because it made express provision for negativing those very faults that in practice we found had arisen. I have not lost confidence, for instance, in gentlemen that I have seen promoted to the bench in the country in which I practised law simply because they happened to belong to the Liberal party. During the years in which I was most active in the practice of my profession, from 1897 onwards, all the appointments to the bench in that country up until 1911 were made by a Liberal government, and made mostly from either defeated candidates or Liberal members of the legislature or of parliament, and I cannot conceive it possible that I could ever stand in the legislature or parliament and say publicly that I had no confidence in the bench because of them.
A et here is a gentleman who was a professional man, and not only a professional man but trained in that profession which usually gives men a wide vision and a large outlook. Those who live in the great outdoors and carry on surveys and have to do with the natural resources of a country, the forest and the stream-no small insular views influence their judgment in the main. They are men accustomed to seeing the wide horizons, the deep forests, the great lakes and rivers, and they usually have wide and large views of the country and of their responsibilities as citizens. That gentleman was appointed to this position. It is true he had been the candidate of the Conservative party and an organizer in a small way in the district in which he lived. He was appointed and took the oath of office, and there stands the challenge that was made by the Minister of Marine and which has not been answered. There is yet to arise any living man who has said that since he took that oath of office he has acted in any way as a partisan. Think of the effect, not of an ordinary member of this house, but of a gentleman who for years was a minister of the crown, with all the authority that attaches to an exMinister of Justice, standing in his place and making the condemnation he did of this gen-

Radio Broadcasting Act
tleman. I say that that strikes at the very foundation of confidence. Then we have the magnificent spectacle to-night of a member of the opposition standing in his place and saying that his confidence in the commission was shaken because the chairman was not shaved, and deriding his whiskers. That is what parliament has fallen to. Now, one can ask oneself the question, in all seriousness, whether under those circumstances it might not be fair to look at the merits of this bill, just as it was presented to this house, with no ulterior object or motive. The letter dated May 5 which was read by the minister this morning suggested

I say suggested, because there was no endeavour to lecture this parliament-with a frankness which I thought did credit to the gentleman, means by which he believed certain purposes could be achieved.
I said this afternoon what I desire to repeat to-night, that in as far as section 1 is concerned I proposed to ask the Civil Service Commission if they have any suggestion to make as to how that situation could be met. For I say, in all frankness, that those who are charged with the responsibility should be able to select the instruments to effect their purposes, and if they cannot do it as to technical men, if they cannot get a broadcasting program without the assistance of the Civil Service Commission, what is going to happen? Do they have to have the approval of the Civil Service Commission before they may employ a singer, or a pianist, or a flute player?
The same old story.

Where was he born, and why-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If you are going to ask all these questions you are going to have a complete failure. Can anybody imagine in the British House of Commons questions of that kind being asked with respect to their broadcasting corporation? There is a pattern to follow. We are endeavouring at least to make our institution worthy of it. I say in all seriousness, that I cannot conceive it possible that there could be in the British House of Commons a discussion such as has taken place this afternoon and evening with respect to our broadcasting legislation. It will be recalled that recently, in December, they did appoint new commissioners. Lady Snowden was appointed, and she was replaced by a Mrs. Hamilton. I forget who the other appointee happened to be, but I remember seeing it in the press. A letter was written to the press saying that this was not the fair thing to do, that the government had acted improperly. A dignified protest was made on behalf of Lady Snowden, and that was the end of it. That is the position. Anyone who follows the press of that country knows it.
I suggest that if we are going to give the radio commission a start, let us at least give it a chance. That is all I have asked this afternoon; that is all I have said. The protests which have been made by hon. members opposite would indicate that their love for it was so great they were willing to destroy it. They indulged in such violent criticisms of the commission as to arouse lack of confidence in and public suspicion as to the motives behind the operations of the commission in regard to this property. Not a tittle of evidence has been adduced in this committee by any person-I repeat, by any person

that in doing their work they were actuated by political motives.
So far as this section is concerned, I asked before dinner that it should stand in order that an opportunity might be afforded to consult with the 'Civil Service Commission to prepare a clause that would protect the commission on the one hand, and ensure that this body which we have set up might be able successfully to function and discharge the duties of a national broadcasting organization.

My right hon. friend has said that as a former Minister of Justice I must know that judges have been appointed to the bench who were active in their respective political parties before their appointments, and that they are good judges. Of course, Mr. Chairman, but you will remember that last year we discussed the bill, and were all intent on having an impartial body. We wanted to have something 
in which the whole country would have confidence. It was suggested to the right hon. gentleman that the appointment of the members of the board might be made after consultation among the leaders of the different groups in the house. My right hon. friend said he would consider that suggestion, but if it were not accepted at least we could rely upon his statement that the appointments would be absolutely non-political. The members of that commission have to deal with something which is very important to every Canadian citizen. The broadcasting business has become part of the very life of all citizens of Canada. We all want to have a fair, square and impartial deal about it. It was the duty of the government to have on the commission men in whom everyone would have confidence. I still say that the appointment to the commission, as -representing an important part of the citizenship of Canada, of a gentleman against whom I say nothing, but who was an active politician, who had not only been a candidate but had been organizer for his party in my own district for many years, for many successive elections, whose words I have myself heard on the radio abusing the party of which I am a member- I say that appointment was not keeping faith with what was said in the house last year when the house voted unanimously to enact the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act. I have nothing to withdraw of what I have said in that respect. I only hope that circumstances will be such that the confidence of the country in the radio board can be restored.
Oh, oh.
